Plan view of the segmented cam ring alone, removed from the frame, its two segments coupled, viewed along the axis of the ring from the same side as FIG. 1 is viewed, so the hinge end is at the left and the latch end at the right. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the meeting surfaces at the two joints, the even spacing of the three slots and their common tilt, the segment on which the ring drive face 36 lies and its position on the outer boundary, and the length of that face.

A flat annulus at the centre of the drawing area is the segmented cam ring 20. It is bounded by one inner circular boundary and one outer circular boundary. The region within the inner boundary is open, and between the two boundaries the face of the annulus toward the viewer is flat and unbroken except where the three slots described below open in it.

Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments. The upper segment is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower segment is the second cam ring segment 24.

At the left joint the ends of the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet along complementary surfaces facing circumferentially, the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26.

At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

Three elongated openings are formed in the annulus and open at the face toward the viewer, one near the top, one at the lower left and one at the lower right. Each is an oblique slot 34, a long narrow opening lying within the width of the annulus and inclined to the radius at its own position, so one end is nearer the inner boundary and the other nearer the outer boundary. The three slots are evenly spaced and identically formed, so that turning the ring a third of a turn carries each slot onto the next and all three tilt the same way about the ring: in each slot the end nearer the inner boundary lies counterclockwise of the end nearer the outer boundary.

The ring drive face 36 is a short flat on the outer boundary of the lower segment, the second cam ring segment 24, just below the right joint. There the outer boundary is interrupted by a single straight edge running between two points of that boundary that lie near one another, slanting inward toward that joint and cutting a little material from the segment. Elsewhere the outer boundary of both segments is circular.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 20 segmented cam ring: target the outer boundary of the annulus in the upper right.
- 22 first cam ring segment: target well inside the upper segment.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target well inside the lower segment.
- 26 complementary coupling faces at the hinge end: target the surfaces meeting at the left joint.
- 28 complementary coupling faces at the latch end: target the meeting surfaces at the right joint.
- 34 oblique slot: target well inside the opening near the top.
- 36 ring drive face: target the straight flat near the right joint.

# FIG. 3

Enlarged fragmentary section through one jaw carriage, the cutting plane containing that carriage's radial direction and the frame axis, the view's left being the axial side from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top; the axis direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the carriage return spring 44, the direction in which the annular guide 18 opens, and the way the oblique slot 34 is formed in the segmented cam ring 20.

A hatched body in section spans the upper part of the view, with a groove in its right portion and a channel in its left portion, the two meeting.

The groove is bounded by the body above and below, closed at its right and open toward the left; its proportions are shown schematically. That groove is the annular guide 18.

A hatched block lies in the groove, filling it radially with a small running clearance above and below. That block is the segmented cam ring 20. A narrow rectangular opening runs into the block from its left face and closes within it toward the right. That opening is the oblique slot 34. Hatched material of the block lies above the opening, below it, and right of its closed end. Its position in the block and its depth are shown schematically.

The channel runs downward from the groove mouth and opens at the underside of the body. That channel is the radial guide 38.

A hatched block lies in the channel and fills its width, its lower end projecting below the body. That block is the jaw carriage 30. A post extends to the right from its upper end, through the groove mouth and into the opening in the block in the groove, its upper and lower sides facing the sides of that opening. That post is the follower 32.

A compression spring drawn as a zigzag line acts between the jaw carriage 30 and the frame body, urging that carriage upward, that is, radially outward. That spring is the carriage return spring 44.

Below the body, a further body hangs from the lower end of the jaw carriage 30 on a small circle, a pivot shown schematically. That body is the jaw pad 40, its lower face a concave arc.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 18 annular guide: target the groove wall above the block lying in it.
- 20 segmented cam ring: target the hatching of the block lying in the groove.
- 30 jaw carriage: target the hatching of the block in the channel.
- 32 follower: target well inside the post.
- 34 oblique slot: target the open space of the opening, right of the post.
- 38 radial guide: target the right wall of the channel that receives the jaw carriage 30.
- 40 jaw pad: target well inside the body hanging below the jaw carriage 30.
- 44 carriage return spring: target the zigzag line.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, closed, parts shown in section, viewed along the frame axis from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the housing and cavity, the attitude of the latch handle 50 in the over-center position, the frame-wall interruption, the length of the ring drive face 36, the width of the gap between the frame bodies, the pivot mounting of the latch handle 50, the opening it passes through and its outline, the direction in which the wedge 52 advances against the ring drive face 36 and the resulting sense of movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 drawn as one spring symbol.

At the lower left a hatched body holds a hatched arcuate band from the left; at the lower right a second holds a like band from the right. A narrow gap separates the bodies, and in it the band ends meet along complementary surfaces in contact. Both bands are the segmented cam ring 20.

The frame wall radially outside the left band is interrupted, exposing its upper side; near the right end that side runs as a straight surface slanting down to the right, the ring drive face 36.

Above the gap a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity opening downward over that face.

A block, the wedge 52, lies in the cavity; its lower left face slants at the same angle as the ring drive face 36 and bears on it, so downward movement drives the band left.

Above it the force-limiting spring stack 54 is a zigzag line rising from the wedge 52.

The latch handle 50 is an elongated lever, shown schematically as a straight bar of even width ending at a straight tip. It is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the cavity's upper right, a short arm reaching from that pivot down and left onto the upper end of that stack. # FIG. 6

Enlarged fragmentary detail of the latch-end joint of the clamp, viewed along the axis of the frame from the same side as FIG. 1, with the wall of the frame nearest the viewer broken away over the region shown so that the ends of the two cam ring segments are visible. In this view the circumferential direction of the frame runs vertically and the radial direction horizontally, radially outward toward the right. The view is confined to the two frame ends at this joint and to the two segment ends. Cut frame material carries section hatching and the two segment ends are drawn in outline without hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the extent of the region, the proportions of the bodies, the slight curvature of the upright edges, the form of the meeting surfaces, and the width of the gap.

Two hatched bodies stand one above the other, one filling the upper part of the view and one filling the lower part, with a narrow horizontal gap between them that runs the full width of the view. The upper body is the latch end of the first frame half 10 and the lower body is the latch end of the second frame half 12.

Each of the two bodies is a single body of hatched material, bounded on the left and on the right by upright edges that curve slightly, and ending toward the gap in a straight horizontal end face reaching from its left edge to its right edge.

A recess is formed in the end face of each body and opens into the gap, one in the upper body opening downward and one in the lower body opening upward. Each recess is set back from the left and the right edge of its body, so hatched frame material stands on both sides of it.

An unhatched block sits in each recess and projects from it into the gap. The block held in the upper body and projecting downward is the first cam ring segment 22, and the block held in the lower body and projecting upward is the second cam ring segment 24. The two blocks are of the same width and stand in line with one another.

Midway across the gap the lower end face of the first cam ring segment 22 and the upper end face of the second cam ring segment 24 meet along complementary horizontal surfaces in contact, so the two blocks read as one upright body interrupted at the joint. Those meeting surfaces are the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 10 first frame half: target the hatching of the upper body, left of the recess in it.
- 12 second frame half: target the hatching of the lower body, left of the recess in it.
- 22 first cam ring segment: target well inside the upper unhatched block.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target well inside the lower unhatched block.
- 28 complementary coupling faces at the latch end: target the meeting surfaces midway across the gap.

# FIG. 3

Enlarged fragmentary section through one jaw carriage, the cutting plane containing that carriage's radial direction and the frame axis, the view's left being the axial side from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top; the axis direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the carriage return spring 44, the direction in which the annular guide 18 opens, and the way the oblique slot 34 appears as a notch in the segmented cam ring 20 at this plane.

A hatched body in section spans the upper part of the view, with a groove in its right portion and a channel in its left portion, the two meeting.

The groove is bounded by the body above and below, closed at its right and open toward the left; its proportions are shown schematically. That groove is the annular guide 18.

A hatched block lies in the groove, filling it radially with a small running clearance above and below. That block is the segmented cam ring 20. One short rectangular notch is cut into that block from its left face and stops within it, and apart from that notch the block is solid and hatched throughout. That notch is the oblique slot 34. Hatched material of the block lies above the notch, below it, and right of its closed end. The position of the notch in the block and its depth are shown schematically.

The channel runs downward from the groove mouth and opens at the underside of the body. That channel is the radial guide 38.

A hatched block lies in the channel and fills its width, its lower end projecting below the body. That block is the jaw carriage 30. A post extends to the right from its upper end, through the groove mouth and into the notch in the block, its upper and lower sides facing the sides of that notch, so the only open space left in the notch is the space around the post. That post is the follower 32.

A compression spring drawn as a zigzag line acts between the jaw carriage 30 and the frame body, urging that carriage upward, that is, radially outward. That spring is the carriage return spring 44.

Below the body, a further body hangs from the lower end of the jaw carriage 30 on a small circle, a pivot shown schematically. That body is the jaw pad 40, its lower face a concave arc.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 18 annular guide: target the groove wall above the block lying in it.
- 20 segmented cam ring: target the hatching of the block lying in the groove.
- 30 jaw carriage: target the hatching of the block in the channel.
- 32 follower: target well inside the post.
- 34 oblique slot: target the open space of the notch, right of the post.
- 38 radial guide: target the right wall of the channel that receives the jaw carriage 30.
- 40 jaw pad: target well inside the body hanging below the jaw carriage 30.
- 44 carriage return spring: target the zigzag line.

# FIG. 3

Enlarged fragmentary section through one jaw carriage, the cutting plane containing that carriage's radial direction and the frame axis, the view's left being the axial side from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top; the axis direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the carriage return spring 44, the direction in which the annular guide 18 opens, and the way the oblique slot 34 appears as a notch in the segmented cam ring 20.

A hatched body in section spans the upper part of the view, with a groove in its right portion and a channel in its left portion, the two meeting.

The groove is bounded by the body above and below, closed at its right and open toward the left; its proportions are shown schematically. That groove is the annular guide 18.

A hatched block lies in the groove, filling it radially with a small running clearance above and below. That block is the segmented cam ring 20. One short rectangular notch is cut into that block from its left face and stops within it; apart from that notch the block is solid and hatched throughout, with hatched material above the notch, below it and right of its closed end. That notch is the oblique slot 34, its position in the block and its depth shown schematically.

The channel runs downward from the groove mouth and opens at the underside of the body. That channel is the radial guide 38.

A hatched block lies in the channel and fills its width, its lower end projecting below the body. That block is the jaw carriage 30. A post extends to the right from its upper end, through the groove mouth and into the notch in the block, its upper and lower sides facing the sides of that notch, so the only open space left in the notch is the space around the post. That post is the follower 32.

A compression spring drawn as a zigzag line acts between the jaw carriage 30 and the frame body, urging that carriage upward, that is, radially outward. That spring is the carriage return spring 44.

Below the body, a further body hangs from the lower end of the jaw carriage 30 on a small circle, a pivot shown schematically. That body is the jaw pad 40, its lower face a concave arc.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 18 annular guide: target the groove wall above the block lying in it.
- 20 segmented cam ring: target the hatching of the block lying in the groove.
- 30 jaw carriage: target the hatching of the block in the channel.
- 32 follower: target well inside the post.
- 34 oblique slot: target the open space of the notch, right of the post.
- 38 radial guide: target the right wall of the channel that receives the jaw carriage 30.
- 40 jaw pad: target well inside the body hanging below the jaw carriage 30.
- 44 carriage return spring: target the zigzag line.

# FIG. 2

Plan view of the segmented cam ring alone, removed from the frame, its two segments coupled, viewed along the ring axis from the same side as FIG. 1, so the hinge end is at the left and the latch end at the right. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the meeting surfaces at the two joints, the even spacing and tilt of the three slots, the segment carrying the ring drive face 36, its position on the outer boundary and its length.

A flat annulus at the centre of the drawing area is the segmented cam ring 20, bounded by one inner circular boundary and one outer circular boundary. The region within the inner boundary is open, and between those two boundaries the face toward the viewer is flat and unbroken except where the three slots below open in it.

Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments: the upper is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower is the second cam ring segment 24.

At the left joint the ends of the two segments meet along complementary surfaces facing circumferentially, the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26.

At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

Three elongated openings open at the face toward the viewer, one near the top, one at the lower left and one at the lower right. Each is an oblique slot 34, a long narrow opening lying within the annulus width and inclined to the radius at its own position, so one end is nearer the inner boundary and the other nearer the outer boundary. The three are evenly spaced and identically formed, so turning the ring a third of a turn carries each onto the next and all three tilt the same way: in each, the end nearer the inner boundary lies counterclockwise of the end nearer the outer boundary.

The ring drive face 36 is a short flat on the outer boundary of the lower segment, the second cam ring segment 24, just below the right joint: there a single straight edge runs between two points of that boundary lying near one another, slanting inward toward that joint and cutting a little material from the segment. Elsewhere the outer boundary of both segments is circular.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 20 segmented cam ring: target the outer boundary in the upper right.
- 22 first cam ring segment: target well inside the upper segment.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target well inside the lower segment.
- 26 complementary coupling faces at the hinge end: target the surfaces meeting at the left joint.
- 28 complementary coupling faces at the latch end: target the meeting surfaces at the right joint.
- 34 oblique slot: target well inside the opening near the top.
- 36 ring drive face: target the straight flat near the right joint.

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, closed, parts shown in section, viewed along the frame axis from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the housing and cavity, the frame-wall interruption, the length of the ring drive face 36, the gap width between the frame bodies, the attitude of the latch handle 50 in the over-center position, its pivot mounting, outline, opening and the short arm by which it acts on the stack, the direction in which the wedge 52 advances and the resulting sense of movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 drawn as one spring symbol.

At the lower left a hatched body holds a hatched arcuate band from the left; at the lower right a second holds a like band from the right. A narrow gap separates the bodies, and in it the band ends meet along complementary surfaces in contact. Both bands are the segmented cam ring 20.

Above the gap a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity opening downward over that face.

From that pivot to its outer end it is one straight bar of even width, its two long edges straight and parallel, its outer end closed by a straight edge square across the bar. A separate short arm on the same pivot reaches down and left onto the upper end of that stack.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from that stack through a hole in the top wall.

# FIG. 6

Enlarged fragmentary detail of the latch-end joint of the clamp, viewed along the axis of the frame from the same side as FIG. 1, with the wall of the frame nearest the viewer broken away over the region shown so that the ends of the two cam ring segments are visible. In this view the circumferential direction of the frame runs vertically and the radial direction horizontally, radially outward toward the right. The view is confined to the two frame ends at this joint and to the two segment ends. Cut frame material carries section hatching and the two segment ends are drawn in outline without hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the extent of the region, the proportions of the bodies, the slight curvature of the upright edges, the form of the meeting surfaces, and the width of the gap.

Two hatched bodies stand one above the other, one filling the upper part of the view and one filling the lower part, with a narrow horizontal gap between them that runs the full width of the view. The upper body is the latch end of the first frame half 10 and the lower body is the latch end of the second frame half 12.

Each of the two bodies is a single body of hatched material, bounded on the left and on the right by upright edges that curve slightly, and ending toward the gap in a straight horizontal end face reaching from its left edge to its right edge.

A recess is formed in the end face of each body and opens into the gap, one in the upper body opening downward and one in the lower body opening upward. Each recess is set back from the left and the right edge of its body, so hatched frame material stands on both sides of it.

An unhatched block sits in each recess and projects from it into the gap. The block held in the upper body and projecting downward is the first cam ring segment 22, and the block held in the lower body and projecting upward is the second cam ring segment 24. The two blocks are of the same width and stand in line with one another.

Midway across the gap the lower end face of the first cam ring segment 22 and the upper end face of the second cam ring segment 24 meet along complementary horizontal surfaces in contact, so the two blocks read as one upright body interrupted at the joint. Those meeting surfaces are the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

# FIG. 2

Plan view of the segmented cam ring alone, removed from the frame, its two segments coupled, viewed along the ring axis from the same side as FIG. 1, so the hinge end is at the left and the latch end at the right. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the meeting surfaces at the two joints, the even spacing and tilt of the three slots, the segment carrying the ring drive face 36, its position on the outer boundary and its length.

A flat annulus at the centre of the drawing area is the segmented cam ring 20, bounded by one inner circular boundary and one outer circular boundary. The region within the inner boundary is open, and between those two boundaries the face toward the viewer is flat and unbroken except where the three slots below open in it.

Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments: the upper is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower is the second cam ring segment 24.

At the left joint the ends of the two segments meet along complementary surfaces facing circumferentially, the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26.

At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

# FIG. 6

Enlarged fragmentary detail of the latch-end joint of the clamp, viewed along the axis of the frame from the same side as FIG. 1, with the wall of the frame nearest the viewer broken away over the region shown so that the ends of the two cam ring segments are visible. In this view the circumferential direction of the frame runs vertically and the radial direction horizontally, radially outward toward the right. The view is confined to the two frame ends at this joint and the two segment ends. Cut frame material carries section hatching and the two segment ends are drawn in outline without hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the extent of the region, the proportions of the bodies, the curvature of the upright edges, the form of the meeting surfaces, and the gap width.

Two hatched bodies stand one above the other, one filling the upper part of the view and one filling the lower part, with a narrow horizontal gap between them that runs the full width of the view. The upper body is the latch end of the first frame half 10 and the lower body is the latch end of the second frame half 12.

Each of the two bodies is a single body of hatched material, bounded on the left and on the right by upright edges that curve slightly, and ending toward the gap in a straight horizontal end face reaching from its left edge to its right edge.

A recess is formed in the end face of each body and opens into the gap, one in the upper body opening downward and one in the lower body opening upward. Each recess is set back from the left and the right edge of its body, so hatched frame material stands on both sides of it.

An unhatched block sits in each recess and projects from it into the gap. The block held in the upper body and projecting downward is the first cam ring segment 22, and the block held in the lower body and projecting upward is the second cam ring segment 24. The two blocks are of the same width and stand in line.

Midway across the gap the lower end face of the first cam ring segment 22 and the upper end face of the second cam ring segment 24 meet along complementary horizontal surfaces in contact, so the two blocks read as one upright body interrupted at the joint. All five failing sheets are addressed in the briefs, and every brief is back under the 2800-character limit (2797, 2799, 2790, 2795, 1945, 2797). No application text, claim, numeral definition, or embodiment changed.

**FIG. 1 - shared anchor coordinates for 90 and 100.** The two leaders now target clearly separated loci: 100 goes to the outer circle bounding the frame body at the upper left, expressly away from the pipe, and 90 goes to the interior of the central circle inside the frame body's inner boundary.

**FIG. 2 - extra concentric contour, wrong slot handedness, doubled and over-long drive face.** The annulus is now stated positively as bounded by one inner and one outer circular boundary, with the face between them flat and unbroken except where the slots open in it. The three slots are described as evenly spaced and identically formed, so a third of a turn carries each onto the next, which forces the shared tilt, with the counterclockwise handedness restated. The drive face is now a short flat formed by a single straight edge running between two nearby points of the outer boundary, so it cannot render as a long chord or a sliver.

**FIG. 3 - phantom tapering bar inside the cam ring block.** The slot at this plane is now one short rectangular notch cut from the block's left face, with the block solid and hatched apart from it, and the follower post fills that notch so the only open space left is around the post.

**FIG. 4 - bent, tapering handle with an oblique tip.** The handle is now described as one straight bar of even width from the pivot to its outer end, edges straight and parallel, end closed square across the bar, with the short arm that acts on the spring stack called out as a separate element on the same pivot, so the bar itself carries no bend or width change.

**FIG. 6 - four hatched bodies, straight boundaries, segments in a central channel, unreliable numeral recovery.** Rewritten around a simpler composition: two single hatched bodies, upper and lower, each bounded left and right by slightly curved upright edges, each with a recess in its end face opening into the gap, and an unhatched block sitting in each recess and projecting into the gap, the two meeting midway at the coupling faces. Each frame half remains one body holding one segment, which is what the description states.

To pay for the added corrective geometry I removed invented rendering constraints rather than required structure: "of substantial width", "knuckle", "wholly", redundant hedges, and verbose phrasing across the five sheets. The prior-art index is still empty and no search was run, so the Background carries no citations and the art available to this draft may be incomplete.

FIG. 1 now sends the leaders for 90 and 100 to clearly separated loci. FIG. 2 states the annulus as bounded by exactly one inner and one outer circular boundary with a flat unbroken face between them, makes the three slots evenly spaced and identically formed so a third of a turn carries each onto the next and all three must share the counterclockwise handedness, and rebuilds the ring drive face as a short flat cut by a single straight edge between two nearby points of the outer boundary. Plan view of the assembled split pipe clamp, closed around a pipe, viewed along the pipe axis. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area.

A circle at the centre of the drawing area is the pipe 90, seen end on.

An annular frame body surrounds the pipe 90, bounded by an inner circle spaced outward from it and an outer circle.

Two radial joint lines, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annular frame body into two semicircular bodies: the upper is the first frame half 10 and the lower is the second frame half 12.

At the left joint is the hinge 14, drawn schematically as a small circle on that joint line with a short block reaching to it from each frame end.

Each jaw carriage 30 carries at its inner end a separate member, the jaw pad 40, joined at a small circle, a pivot shown schematically; its inner face is a concave arc meeting the pipe 90.

A short broken cutting-plane line lies in the upper part of the view, on the radial centre line of the topmost jaw carriage 30. The ring drive face 36 is a short flat on the outer boundary of the lower segment, the second cam ring segment 24, just below the right joint: there a single straight edge runs between two points of that boundary lying near one another, slanting inward toward that joint and cutting a little material from the segment. # FIG. 2

Plan view of the segmented cam ring alone, removed from the frame, its two segments coupled, viewed along the ring axis from the same side as FIG. 1, so the hinge end is at the left and the latch end at the right. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the meeting surfaces at the two joints, the even spacing and tilt of the three slots, the segment carrying the ring drive face 36, its position on the outer boundary and its length.

A flat annulus at the centre of the drawing area is the segmented cam ring 20, bounded by one inner circular boundary and one outer circular boundary. The region within the inner boundary is open, and between those two boundaries the face of the ring is flat and unbroken except where the three slots below open in it.

Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments: the upper is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower is the second cam ring segment 24.

At the left joint the ends of the two segments meet along complementary surfaces facing circumferentially, the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26.

At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

Three elongated openings are formed in the annulus, one near the top, one at the lower left, one at the lower right. Each is an oblique slot 34, a long narrow opening lying within the annulus width and inclined to the radius at its own position, so one end is nearer the inner boundary, the other the outer. The three are evenly spaced and identically formed, so turning the ring a third of a turn carries each onto the next and all three tilt the same way: in each, the end nearer the inner boundary lies counterclockwise of the end nearer the outer boundary.

The ring drive face 36 is a short flat on the outer boundary of the lower segment, the second cam ring segment 24, just below the right joint: there a single straight edge runs between two points of that boundary lying near one another, slanting inward toward that joint and cutting a little material from the segment. Elsewhere both outer boundaries are circular.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 20 segmented cam ring: target the outer boundary of the annulus in the upper right.
- 22 first cam ring segment: target well inside the upper segment.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target well inside the lower segment.
- 26 complementary coupling faces at the hinge end: target the surfaces meeting at the left joint.
- 28 complementary coupling faces at the latch end: target the meeting surfaces at the right joint.
- 34 oblique slot: target well inside the opening near the top.
- 36 ring drive face: target the slanting surface near the right joint.

content.text:
The one verified defect is fixed with the two-line correction the review specified, plus the knock-on wording it forces in FIG. 2.

**Annular guide opening side (FIG. 1, FIG. 3, FIG. 5, FIG. 6).** The guide now opens on the axial side away from the FIG. 1 viewer:
- `figures/FIG-1.md`: the cutting-plane arrows now point to the right of the view.
- `figures/FIG-3.md`: the view's right is now the axial side from which FIG. 1 is viewed.

With that flip, FIG. 3's groove closed at the right and open toward the left, FIG. 5's identical groove statement, FIG. 6's break-away of the near frame wall, and FIG. 1's plain annular frame face all describe one consistent solid. FIG. 3's own chain still holds internally: the groove mouth, the channel that meets it, and the post reaching rightward into the notch are unchanged.

**FIG. 2 knock-on.** The brief said the slots "open at the face toward the viewer" while being viewed from the same side as FIG. 1. Under the corrected convention that face is the closed one, so the wording would have reinstated the same contradiction. # FIG. 3

Enlarged fragmentary section through one jaw carriage, the cutting plane containing that carriage's radial direction and the frame axis, the view's right being the axial side from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top; the axis runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the carriage return spring 44, the direction in which the annular guide 18 opens, and the way the oblique slot 34 appears as a notch in the segmented cam ring 20.

A hatched body in section spans the upper part of the view, with a groove in its right portion and a channel in its left, the two meeting.

The groove is bounded by the body above and below, closed at its right and open toward the left; its proportions shown schematically. That groove is the annular guide 18.

A hatched block lies in the groove, filling it radially with a small running clearance above and below. That block is the segmented cam ring 20. One short rectangular notch is cut into that block from its left face and stops within it; apart from that notch the block is solid and hatched throughout, with hatched material above the notch, below it and right of its closed end. That notch is the oblique slot 34, its position in the block and its depth shown schematically.

The channel runs downward from the groove mouth and opens at the underside of the body. That channel is the radial guide 38.

A hatched block lies in the channel and fills its width, its lower end projecting below the body. That block is the jaw carriage 30. A post extends to the right from its upper end, through the groove mouth and into that notch, its upper and lower sides facing the notch sides, so the only open space left in the notch is around the post. That post is the follower 32.

A compression spring drawn as a zigzag line acts between the jaw carriage 30 and the frame body, urging that carriage upward, radially outward. That spring is the carriage return spring 44.

Below the body, a further body hangs from the lower end of the jaw carriage 30 on a small circle, a pivot shown schematically. That body is the jaw pad 40, its lower face a concave arc.

# FIG. 3

Enlarged fragmentary section through one jaw carriage, the cutting plane containing that carriage's radial direction and the frame axis, the view's right being the axial side from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top; the axis runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the carriage return spring 44, the direction in which the annular guide 18 opens, and the way the oblique slot 34 appears as an opening through the segmented cam ring 20.

A hatched body in section spans the upper part of the view, with a groove in its right portion and a channel in its left, the two meeting.

The groove is bounded by the body above and below, closed at its right and open toward the left; its proportions shown schematically. That groove is the annular guide 18.

A hatched block lies in the groove, filling it radially with a small running clearance above and below. That block is the segmented cam ring 20. One short rectangular opening passes through that block from its left face to its right face; apart from that opening the block is solid and hatched throughout, with hatched material above the opening and below it. That opening is the oblique slot 34, its position in the block shown schematically.

The channel runs downward from the groove mouth and opens at the underside of the body. That channel is the radial guide 38.

A hatched block lies in the channel and fills its width, its lower end projecting below the body. That block is the jaw carriage 30. A post extends to the right from its upper end, through the groove mouth and into that opening, its upper and lower sides facing the sides of the opening, so the only open space left in the opening is around the post. That post is the follower 32.

A compression spring drawn as a zigzag line acts between the jaw carriage 30 and the frame body, urging that carriage upward, radially outward. That spring is the carriage return spring 44.

Below the body, a further body hangs from the lower end of the jaw carriage 30 on a small circle, a pivot shown schematically. That body is the jaw pad 40, its lower face a concave arc.

# FIG. 1

Plan view of the assembled split pipe clamp, closed around a pipe, viewed along the pipe axis. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area.

A circle at the centre of the drawing area is the pipe 90, seen end on.

An annular frame body surrounds the pipe 90, bounded by an inner circle spaced outward from it and an outer circle.

Two radial joint lines, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annular frame body into two semicircular bodies: the upper is the first frame half 10 and the lower is the second frame half 12.

At the left joint is the hinge 14, drawn schematically as a small circle on that joint line with a short block reaching to it from each frame end.

At the right joint is the latch 16, drawn schematically as a rectangular block outside the frame body bridging both frame ends, with an elongated lever extending away from it. The latch 16 is in its over-center position, the pipe 90 clamped; the lever attitude is shown schematically.

Three jaw carriages 30 are spaced around the annular frame body, one at the top, one at the lower left and one at the lower right, each crossing its inner boundary and reaching inward toward the pipe 90. The topmost lies on the first frame half 10 and the other two on the second frame half 12; shown schematically.

Each jaw carriage 30 carries at its inner end a separate member, the jaw pad 40, joined at a small circle, a pivot shown schematically; its inner face is a concave arc meeting the pipe 90.

A short broken cutting-plane line lies in the upper part of the view, on the radial centre line of the topmost jaw carriage 30. Its outer end lies just outside the outer circle of the frame body and its inner end stops where the concave face of the jaw pad 40 of that carriage meets the pipe 90. A short arrow at each end points horizontally to the right of the view, both to the same side of the line, giving the direction in which the section of FIG. 3 is viewed. Each end also carries the numeral 3 as the section designation, set just outside that end beside its arrow, so the line reads as line 3-3; it is not a reference numeral.

# FIG. 3

Enlarged fragmentary section through one jaw carriage, the cutting plane containing that carriage's radial direction and the frame axis, the view's right being the axial side from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top; the axis runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the carriage return spring 44, the direction in which the annular guide 18 opens, and the way the oblique slot 34 appears as an opening through the segmented cam ring 20.

A hatched body in section spans the upper part of the view, with a groove in its right portion and a channel in its left, the two meeting.

The groove is bounded by the body above and below, closed at its right and open toward the left; its proportions shown schematically. That groove is the annular guide 18.

A hatched block lies in the groove, filling it radially with a small running clearance above and below. That block is the segmented cam ring 20. One short rectangular opening passes through that block from its left face to its right face; apart from that opening the block is solid and hatched throughout, with hatched material above the opening and below it. That opening is the oblique slot 34, its position in the block shown schematically.

The channel runs downward from the groove mouth and opens at the underside of the body. That channel is the radial guide 38.

A hatched block lies in the channel and fills its width, its lower end projecting below the body. That block is the jaw carriage 30. A post extends to the right from its upper end, through the groove mouth and into that opening, its upper and lower sides facing the sides of the opening, so the only open space left in the opening is around the post. That post is the follower 32.

A compression spring drawn as a zigzag line acts between the jaw carriage 30 and the frame body, urging that carriage upward, radially outward. That spring is the carriage return spring 44.

Below the body, a further body hangs from the lower end of the jaw carriage 30 on a small circle, a pivot shown schematically. That body is the jaw pad 40, its lower face a concave arc.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 18 annular guide: target the groove wall above the block in it.
- 20 segmented cam ring: target the hatching of the block in the groove.
- 30 jaw carriage: target the hatching of the block in the channel.
- 32 follower: target well inside the post.
- 34 oblique slot: target the open space of the opening, right of the post.
- 38 radial guide: target the right wall of the channel holding the jaw carriage 30.
- 40 jaw pad: target well inside the body below the jaw carriage 30.
- 44 carriage return spring: target the zigzag line.

# FIG. 1

Plan view of the assembled split pipe clamp, closed around a pipe, viewed along the pipe axis. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area.

A circle at the centre of the drawing area is the pipe 90, seen end on.

An annular frame body surrounds the pipe 90, bounded by an inner circle spaced outward from it and an outer circle.

Two radial joint lines, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annular frame body into two semicircular bodies: the upper is the first frame half 10 and the lower is the second frame half 12.

At the left joint is the hinge 14, drawn schematically as a small circle on that joint line with a short block reaching to it from each frame end.

At the right joint is the latch 16, drawn schematically as a rectangular block outside the frame body bridging both frame ends, with an elongated lever extending away from it, in its over-center position, the pipe 90 clamped; the lever attitude is shown schematically.

Three jaw carriages 30 are spaced around the annular frame body, one at the top, one at the lower left and one at the lower right, each seen only radially inside the inner circle of that body, which runs unbroken past them, and each reaching inward toward the pipe 90. The topmost lies on the first frame half 10, the others on the second frame half 12; shown schematically.

Each jaw carriage 30 carries at its inner end a separate member, the jaw pad 40, joined at a small circle, a pivot shown schematically; its inner face is a concave arc meeting the pipe 90.

A short broken cutting-plane line lies in the upper part of the view, on the radial centre line of the topmost jaw carriage 30. Its outer end lies just outside the outer circle of the frame body and its inner end stops where the concave face of that carriage's jaw pad 40 meets the pipe 90. A short arrow at each end points horizontally to the right of the view, both to the same side of the line, giving the direction in which FIG. 3 is viewed. Each end also carries the numeral 3 as the section designation, set just outside that end beside its arrow, so the line reads as line 3-3; it is not a reference numeral.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 100 split pipe clamp: target the outer circle of the frame body at the upper left, away from the pipe 90.
- 10 first frame half: target well inside the upper semicircular body.
- 12 second frame half: target well inside the lower semicircular body.
- 14 hinge: target the small circle at the left joint.
- 16 latch: target the rectangular block bridging the right joint.
- 30 jaw carriage: target well inside the topmost carriage block.
- 40 jaw pad: target well inside the member at the topmost carriage inner end.
- 90 pipe: target the interior of the central circle, inside the inner circle.

Both findings are fixed, entirely inside the figure briefs, with no change to any application text.

**FIG. 2 / FIG. 3 slot-face contradiction (major).** The oblique slot 34 is now a through opening in FIG. 3, matching FIG. 2's depiction of the slots as openings in the ring:
- The schematic declaration now reads "the way the oblique slot 34 appears as an opening through the segmented cam ring 20."
- The ring block now carries one short rectangular opening passing from its left face to its right face, with hatched material above and below it, and the depth hedge is gone since there is no longer a blind depth.
- The follower post enters that opening, its upper and lower sides facing the sides of the opening, so the only open space left is around the post.
- The numeral 34 endpoint names the opening.

No claim, description, or numeral change was needed: the specification and claims say only that the follower is received in the slot and bears against its sides, and state no depth.

**FIG. 1 jaw carriages drawn over the frame face (minor).** FIG. 1 now says each jaw carriage 30 is seen only radially inside the inner circle of the frame body, which runs unbroken past them, and each reaches inward toward the pipe. That matches the closed near wall FIG. 3 establishes, which already hides the cam ring, slots, and followers. The carriages and jaw pads remain visible where they project inward of the frame body, so the numeral 30 and 40 targets still resolve. I phrased the occlusion positively, as what is visible and what lies behind the wall, rather than as a ban on drawing linework.

To fit the added wording I trimmed FIG. 1 elsewhere without losing geometry: the latch sentence, two phrases in the cutting-line paragraph, and two endpoint descriptions. All six briefs are within the limit at 2787, 2787, 2784, 2795, 1945 and 2798 characters, no numeral moved between sheets, and the claims, detailed description, drawing descriptions, and numeral table are untouched. The prior-art index is still empty and no search was run, so the Background carries no citations and the art available to this draft may be incomplete.

input.summary: Fixed both figure-set inconsistencies left by the earlier axial-side flip, entirely inside the figure briefs. The oblique slot 34 is now a through opening in FIG. 3, passing from the block's left face to its right face with hatched ring material above and below, which matches FIG. 2's depiction of the slots as openings in the ring and removes the contradiction about which axial face they open in. FIG. 1 now shows each jaw carriage 30 only radially inside the inner circle of the frame body, with that circle running unbroken past them, so the view no longer draws the carriages over the same near wall it relies on to hide the cam ring, slots and followers. No claim, description, drawing description, numeral definition or disclosed embodiment changed, since neither the specification nor the claims state any slot depth or any plan-view visibility. All six briefs are within the character limit. Prior art note as the drafting brief requires: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references and no search was run, so the art available to this draft may be incomplete.
reasoning: Both defects were contradictions between figure briefs, so both repairs stayed in figures/. The authority order held: the disclosure says only that each carriage has a follower received in a respective oblique slot, and the description says only that the follower bears against the sides of the slot, so nothing above the briefs constrained the choice and nothing above the briefs had to move.

For the slot, the two sheets could not both be rendered: FIG. 2 showed the slots as openings in the ring face nearest the FIG. 1 viewer, while FIG. 3 made them blind notches entered from the far face with solid material between the slot and that near face. I resolved it in FIG. 3 rather than FIG. 2 because FIG. 3 already declared the slot's appearance and depth to be schematic, while FIG. 2's slot depiction is tied to its joint positions and handedness, which the review verified as consistent with FIG. 4's wedge direction and the resulting inward carriage travel. Reopening FIG. 2 would have put that verified chain at risk for no gain.

Making the slot a through opening also let me delete the depth hedge from FIG. 3, since a through opening has no blind depth to hedge. That is one less renderer-facing qualifier, and it removes the very geometry that produced the phantom tapering bar two rounds ago, because the block is now solid and hatched above and below one opening with nothing left to interpret as a second cavity.

For FIG. 1, the carriages were drawn crossing the inner boundary onto the frame-body face, which is the same face FIG. 3 makes a closed near wall hiding the ring, the slots and the followers. I stated the fix positively, as what the view shows and what lies behind the wall: each carriage is seen only radially inside the inner circle of the frame body, and that circle runs unbroken past them. I deliberately did not write it as a prohibition on drawing part of a carriage over the frame face, because generic negative linework controls are exactly what the drafting rules exclude.

I left the numeral 30 and 40 targets alone. Both resolve to the inward-projecting portion of the topmost carriage and its pad, which stays visible under the corrected wording, so there was no endpoint to move.

The added occlusion wording pushed FIG. 1 to 2821 characters, so I recovered the space from phrasing rather than geometry: the latch sentence was merged, two phrases in the cutting-line paragraph were shortened, and two endpoint descriptions were tightened while keeping the separation between the 90 and 100 targets that an earlier anchor failure required. All six briefs now run 1945 to 2798 characters.

No numeral moved between sheets, so figure coverage stands unchanged at eight, seven, eight, seven, four and five numerals, and every part the description calls visible in a figure is still listed on that sheet.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there was no document to cite, distinguish, or write around, and I invented none. The Background carries no citations for that reason and the claims rest on the inventor's disclosure alone. The feature carrying claim 1 is the drive element divided with the clamp body and recoupled into a single ring by the act of closing the frame halves, through complementary coupling faces at both the hinge end and the latch end, so one latch input at one point on one frame half reaches all three jaw carriages through one kinematic element, and the relationship between the carriages is set by ring geometry rather than by how the clamp is operated. The second is the force-limiting spring stack between latch handle and wedge, which takes up the handle travel remaining after all three pads land instead of driving one jaw deeper, with the indicator pin reporting the state of that stack and not the diameter of the pipe. Background paragraphs 3, 5 and 7 set out the technical problems both answer, in the invention's own vocabulary rather than that of band clamps or two-bolt saddles. Nothing this turn touched the claims or the specification, so scope is unchanged. Because no search was run, none of this is a statement about what the wider art contains.
